ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in $\triangle ABC$, point D is the midpoint of side AB, and $CD = \frac{1}{2}AB$. Prove that: $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Proof: Since point D is the midpoint of side $AB$,\\
$ \therefore AD=BD=\frac{1}{2}AB$,\\
Also since $CD=\frac{1}{2}AB$,\\
$ \therefore AD=BD=CD$,\\
$ \therefore \angle ACD=\angle A$, $\angle BCD=\angle B$.\\
Since $\angle A+\angle B+(\angle ACD+\angle BCD)=180^\circ$,\\
$ \therefore \angle ACD+\angle BCD+(\angle ACD+\angle BCD)=180^\circ$,\\
$ \therefore 2(\angle ACD+\angle BCD)=180^\circ$,\\
$ \therefore \angle ACD+\angle BCD=90^\circ$,\\
which means $\angle ACB=\boxed{90^\circ}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure is triangle ABC, with A at the lower left, C at the lower right, and B at the upper right and roughly located above C; AB is the hypotenuse, BC is approximately vertical, and AC is approximately horizontal. Point D is located on side AB, and line segment CD is drawn from C to D. Then reason: According to the problem statement, D is the midpoint of AB, so AD=DB=AB/2. It is also known that CD=AB/2, therefore AD=DB=CD. Thus the three points A, B, and C all lie on the same circle with D as the center and AD as the radius. In the figure, A, D, and B are collinear, and AD=DB, so AB passes through the circle center D, and A and B are two points on the circle; therefore AB is a diameter of this circle. According to Thales' theorem, the inscribed angle ∠ACB subtended by diameter AB at any point C on the circle is a right angle. Therefore ∠ACB=90°.
